old: “I know he won’t. I know it perfectly well, and now more than ever. And that’s not all. I know something else. Only a few days ago, perhaps just yesterday, he understood for the first time _in earnest_ (underline _in earnest_) that Grushenka may not be joking after all, and really means to marry me. He knows what she’s like; he knows the cat. So do you imagine he’ll give me money to help that along, when he’s mad about her himself? And that isn’t all, either. I can tell you more than that. I know that for the past five days he’s had three thousand drawn from the bank, changed into notes of a hundred roubles, packed into a big envelope, sealed with five seals and tied crosswise with red tape. You see how well informed I am! On the envelope he’s written: ‘To my angel Grushenka, when she will come to me.’ He scrawled it himself, silently and in secret, and nobody knows the money is there except the valet Smerdyakov, whom he trusts as he trusts himself. So for three or four days now he’s been expecting Grushenka. He hopes she’ll come for the money. He’s sent word to her about it, and she’s sent word back that perhaps she’ll come. And if she does go to the old man, can I marry her afterwards? Now you see why I’m here in secret, and what I’m keeping watch for.”

old: “Listen! I took up the case of children only to make my point clearer. As for the other tears of humanity, which soak the earth from its crust to its core, I’ll say nothing about them. I’ve narrowed my subject on purpose. I’m a bug, and I admit in all humility that I can’t understand why the world is arranged the way it is. Men are to blame themselves, I suppose. They were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven, knowing they would be made unhappy. So there’s no need to pity them. All I know, with my pitiful, earthly, Euclidian mind, is that there is suffering and nobody is guilty; that cause follows effect plainly and directly; that everything flows and finds its level. But that’s only Euclidian nonsense, I know it, and I can’t agree to live by it! What comfort is it to me that nobody is guilty, that cause follows effect plainly and directly, and that I know it? I must have justice, or I’ll destroy myself. And not justice in some remote, infinite time and place, but here on earth, where I can see it myself. I have believed in it. I want to see it, and if I’m dead by then, let me rise again. If it all happens without me, that will be too unfair. Surely I didn’t suffer just so that my crimes and my sufferings could manure the ground for somebody else’s future harmony. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion, and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. Every religion in the world is built on this longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children, and what am I to do about them? That’s the question I can’t answer. For the hundredth time I say it: there are masses of questions, but I’ve taken only the children, because in their case what I mean is unanswerably clear. Listen! If everyone has to suffer in order to pay for the eternal harmony, what do children have to do with it? Tell me, please. It’s beyond all understanding why they should suffer, and why they should have to pay for the harmony. Why should they, too, be material to enrich the soil for somebody’s future harmony? I understand solidarity among men in sin. I understand solidarity in retribution, too. But there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it’s really true that they share the responsibility for all their fathers’ crimes, then that truth does not belong to this world, and I can’t comprehend it. Some jester will say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned. But he didn’t grow up, you see. He was torn to pieces by dogs at eight years old. Oh, Alyosha, I’m not blaspheming! I do understand what an upheaval of the universe it will be, when everything in heaven and on earth blends into one hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has lived cries aloud: ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed.’ When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three cry aloud through their tears, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ then, of course, the crown of knowledge will have been reached and everything will be clear. But this is exactly where I stop: I can’t accept that harmony. And while I’m still on earth, I make haste to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, perhaps it really may happen that if I live to see that moment, or rise again to witness it, I too, perhaps, may cry out with the rest, as I watch the mother embrace her child’s torturer, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ But I don’t want to cry it out then. While there’s still time, I hurry to protect myself, and so I renounce the higher harmony altogether. It isn’t worth the tears of that one tortured child, who beat her little chest with her little fist and prayed in her stinking outhouse, with her unatoned tears, to ‘dear, kind God’! It isn’t worth it, because those tears are unatoned for. They have to be atoned for, or there can be no harmony. But how? How will you atone for them? Is it even possible? By avenging them? But what do I care about avenging them? What do I care about a hell for the oppressors? What good can hell do, when those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don’t want any more suffering. And if the suffering of children goes to make up the sum of suffering needed to pay for the truth, then I protest that the truth isn’t worth such a price. I don’t want the mother to embrace the oppressor who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants to. Let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering of her own mother’s heart. But the suffering of her tortured child she has no right to forgive. She can’t forgive the torturer, even if the child forgave him! And if that’s so, if they have no right to forgive, what becomes of harmony? Is there anyone in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and could? I don’t want harmony. Out of love for humanity I don’t want it. I’d rather keep my unavenged suffering. I’d rather stay with my unavenged suffering and my unsatisfied indignation, _even if I were wrong_. Besides, the price of harmony is too high. It’s beyond our means to pay so much to get in. And so I hurry to hand back my entrance ticket, and if I’m an honest man, I’m bound to hand it back as soon as I can. That’s what I’m doing. It isn’t God I don’t accept, Alyosha. I just most respectfully return Him the ticket.”

old: “‘When they receive bread from us, they will see plainly that we take the bread their own hands have made, only to hand it back to them, and that there is no miracle in it. They will see that we do not turn stones into bread. Yet in truth they will be more grateful for receiving it from our hands than for the bread itself! They will remember only too well that in the old days, without our help, even the bread they made turned to stones in their hands, while since they came back to us, the very stones have turned to bread in their hands. Too, too well will they understand the value of complete submission! And until men understand that, they will be unhappy. Who is most to blame that they do not? Speak! Who scattered the flock and sent it wandering down unknown paths? But the flock will gather again and submit once more, and this time it will be for good. Then we shall give them the quiet, humble happiness of weak creatures, which is what they are by nature. Oh, we shall persuade them in the end not to be proud, because You lifted them up and so taught them pride. We shall show them that they are weak, that they are nothing but pitiful children, and that a child’s happiness is the sweetest there is. They will grow timid. They will look to us and press close to us in fear, as chicks do to the hen. They will marvel at us and stand in awe of us. They will take pride in our being so powerful and so clever that we could tame a flock this unruly, thousands of millions strong. They will tremble helplessly when we are angry, their minds will fill with fear, and they will cry as easily as women and children do. But at a sign from us they will turn just as readily to laughter and rejoicing, to happy mirth and childish song. Yes, we shall make them work, but in their free hours we shall arrange their life like a child’s game, with children’s songs and innocent dances. Oh, we shall even let them sin. They are weak and helpless, and they will love us like children because we let them sin. We shall tell them that every sin will be atoned for if it is done with our permission. We let them sin because we love them, we shall say, and the punishment for these sins we take on ourselves. And we shall take it on ourselves, and they will adore us as the saviors who have borne their sins before God. They will keep no secrets from us. We shall permit or forbid them to live with their wives and mistresses, and to have children or not, depending on whether they have obeyed or disobeyed, and they will submit to us gladly and cheerfully. The most painful secrets of their conscience, all, all of them, they will bring to us, and we shall have an answer for all. They will be glad to believe our answer, for it will spare them the great anxiety and the terrible agony they suffer now, having to decide freely for themselves. And all will be happy, all the millions of creatures, except the hundred thousand who rule over them. For only we, who guard the mystery, will be unhappy. There will be thousands of millions of happy babes, and a hundred thousand sufferers who have taken on themselves the curse of the knowledge of good and evil. Peacefully they will die, peacefully they will expire in Your name, and beyond the grave they will find nothing but death. But we shall keep the secret, and for their happiness we shall tempt them on with the reward of heaven and eternity. Though if there were anything in the other world, it certainly would not be for such as they. It is prophesied that You will come again in victory, with Your chosen, the proud and the strong. But we will say that they have saved only themselves, and we have saved everyone. We are told that the harlot who sits upon the beast, holding the _mystery_ in her hands, will be put to shame; that the weak will rise up again, tear her royal purple, and strip her loathsome body bare. But then I will stand up and show You the thousand millions of happy children who have never known sin. And we, who took their sins on ourselves for their happiness, will stand before You and say: “Judge us, if You can and dare.” Know that I do not fear You. Know that I too have been in the wilderness, that I too lived on roots and locusts, that I too prized the freedom You have blessed men with, and that I too was struggling to take my place among Your elect, among the strong and mighty, hungering “to make up the number.” But I woke up, and I refused to serve madness. I turned back and joined the ranks of those _who have corrected Your work_. I left the proud and returned to the humble, for the humble’s happiness. What I tell You will come to pass, and our dominion will be built. I repeat, tomorrow You will see that obedient flock, which at one sign from me will rush to pile the glowing coals around the stake where I shall burn You for coming to hinder us. For if anyone has ever deserved our fires, it is You. Tomorrow I shall burn You. _Dixi._’”

old: In the end the elder’s death came quite unexpectedly. The people gathered around him that last evening knew that his death was near. Still, it was hard to imagine it would come so suddenly. On the contrary, as I said before, his friends saw him that night so seemingly cheerful and talkative that they were convinced his condition had changed for the better, at least for a time. Even five minutes before he died, they said afterwards in amazement, there was no way of foreseeing it. He seemed suddenly to feel a sharp pain in his chest. He went pale and pressed his hands to his heart. Everyone got up from their seats and hurried to him. But though he was in pain, he still looked at them with a smile. He slid slowly from his chair to his knees, then bowed his face to the ground, stretched out his arms, and, as if in joyful ecstasy, praying and kissing the ground, he quietly and joyfully gave up his soul to God.

old: Mihail Makarovitch was not at all efficient at his work, though he did it no worse than many others. To put it plainly, he had little education. He could not always be trusted to know where his official powers ended. He didn’t exactly fail to understand certain reforms of the present reign. Rather, he made glaring blunders when he applied them. This wasn’t because he was especially dull. He was careless, and always too hurried to look into the matter properly.
new: Mihail Makarovitch was not very efficient at his work, though he did it no worse than many others. To put it plainly, he was a man of rather limited education. He could not always be trusted to know where his official powers ended. He didn’t exactly fail to understand certain reforms of the present reign. Rather, he made glaring blunders when he applied them. This wasn’t because he was especially dull. He was careless, and always too hurried to look into the matter properly.

old: “Damn his sorrow! Well, where to now? Do I just go on sitting here?”
new: “Confound his sorrow! Well, where to now? Do I just go on sitting here?”

old: “Yes, I see a vital difference! Any man can be a scoundrel, and perhaps every man is one, but not everyone can be a thief. For that you have to be an arch-scoundrel. Oh, of course, I don’t know how to draw these fine lines ... but a thief is lower than a scoundrel, that’s what I believe. Listen: I carry the money on me for a whole month. Any day I might make up my mind to give it back, and then I’m not a scoundrel anymore. But I can’t make up my mind, you see, though I decide every day, every day I push myself to do it, and still for a whole month I can’t bring myself to it. Is that right, do you think? Is that right?”

old: His main feeling was relief that the murderer was Mitya and not Smerdyakov, though you would have expected the reverse. He did not want to analyze why, and in fact felt a real distaste for prying into his own feelings. He seemed to want to hurry up and forget something. Over the next few days he became convinced of Mitya’s guilt, as he learned how heavy the evidence against him was. Some of it came from unimportant people, Fenya and her mother for example, yet its effect was almost crushing. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern and at Plotnikov’s shop, and the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence looked conclusive. It was the details that did the damage. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers nearly as much as Grigory’s evidence about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa, answering Ivan’s questions, declared that Smerdyakov had lain all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed.” She was a sound sleeper, yet she had woken several times and heard him groaning. “He was groaning the whole time, groaning without a stop.”

old: “What is there left to tell? I was lying there, and I thought I heard the master shout. Just before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly got up and gone out, and then he let out a scream, and after that it was all silent and dark. I lay there waiting, my heart thumping. I couldn’t stand it. In the end I got up and went out. The window on the left, the one facing the garden, was standing open. I stepped over to the left and listened for whether he was sitting in there alive, and I heard the master moving about and sighing. So I knew he was alive. ‘Ech!’ I thought. I went up to the window and called to him, ‘It’s me.’ And he called back, ‘He’s been here, he’s been here; he’s run off.’ He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been. ‘He’s killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,’ he said, and pointed. He was whispering too. ‘Wait a bit,’ I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there was Grigory Vassilyevitch, lying by the wall, covered in blood and out cold. So it’s true, I thought, Dmitri Fyodorovitch really has been here. And on the spot I decided to put an end to it all. Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he was alive, would never know what happened, lying there senseless like that. The one danger was that Marfa Ignatyevna might wake up. I felt that at the time. But the longing to get it done had come over me so badly that I could scarcely breathe. I went back to the window and told the master, ‘She’s here, she’s come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come and wants to be let in.’ And he jumped like a baby. ‘Where is she?’ he gasped, but he couldn’t believe it. ‘She’s standing out there,’ I said. ‘Open up.’ He looked out of the window at me, half believing and half suspicious, and afraid to open. ‘Why, he’s afraid of me now,’ I thought. And it struck me as funny. So I thought of knocking on the window frame, right there before his eyes, with those taps we had agreed on as the sign that Grushenka had come. He didn’t seem to trust my word, but the moment he heard the taps, he ran to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the doorway so I couldn’t get past. ‘Where is she? Where is she?’ He stared at me, shaking all over. ‘Well,’ I thought, ‘if he’s that frightened of me, it looks bad!’ And my legs went weak with fear that he wouldn’t let me in, or would shout, or that Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or that something else would go wrong. I can’t remember now, but I must have stood there pale, facing him. I whispered to him, ‘Why, she’s there, right under the window; how can you not see her?’ ‘Bring her, then, bring her.’ ‘She’s scared,’ I said; ‘the noise frightened her, she’s hiding in the bushes; go and call her yourself from the study.’ He ran to the window and put the candle on the sill. ‘Grushenka,’ he cried, ‘Grushenka, are you there?’ He cried it, but he wouldn’t lean out of the window, and he wouldn’t step away from me, because he was in a panic. He was so frightened he didn’t dare turn his back on me. ‘Why, there she is,’ I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out. ‘There she is; she’s in the bush, laughing at you, can’t you see her?’ All at once he believed it. He was shaking all over—he was terribly crazy about her—and he leaned right out of the window. I snatched up the iron paperweight from his table; you remember it, about three pounds in weight? I swung it and struck him on the top of the skull with the corner. He didn’t even cry out. He just sagged down, and I struck him again, and a third time. By the third blow I knew I had broken his skull. He suddenly rolled over on his back, face up, covered in blood. I looked round. There was no blood on me, not a spot. I wiped the paperweight and put it back. Then I went to the ikons, took the money out of the envelope, and dropped the envelope on the floor with the pink ribbon next to it. I went out into the garden, shaking all over, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it—you know the hollow. I’d marked it long before and left a rag and a scrap of paper ready inside. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and shoved it deep into the hole. And there it stayed for over two weeks. I took it out afterwards, when I came out of the hospital. I went back to my bed and lay down, thinking, ‘If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, it may turn out badly for me. But if he’s not killed and he recovers, it’ll be first-rate, because then he’ll swear that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was here, and so Dmitri Fyodorovitch must have killed him and taken the money.’ Then I began to groan, from suspense and impatience, to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as I could. At last she got up and ran to me, but when she saw that Grigory Vassilyevitch wasn’t there, she ran out, and I heard her scream in the garden. That set it all in motion, and it put my mind at rest.”

old: “Listen ...” said Ivan, who seemed bewildered again and was struggling to catch hold of something. “Listen. There are many questions I wanted to ask you, but I’ve forgotten them ... I keep forgetting, and I get muddled. Yes. Tell me this, at least. Why did you tear open the envelope and leave it lying on the floor? Why didn’t you just carry the envelope off?... When you were telling me, I thought you spoke of it as if it were the right thing to do ... but why, I can’t understand....”

old: “Allow me to ask,” the counsel for the defense began, with the friendliest and even a respectful smile, “you are, of course, the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, _The Life of the Deceased Elder, Father Zossima_, published by the diocesan authorities, full of deep and religious reflections and opening with an excellent, devout dedication to the bishop, I have just read with such pleasure?”

old: No, I can never forget those moments. She began telling her story. She told everything, the whole episode that Mitya had told Alyosha, her bowing to the ground, and her reason for it. She told about her father and how she went to Mitya. Not in one word, not in a single hint, did she let on that Mitya himself, through her sister, had suggested that they “send Katerina Ivanovna” to fetch the money. She generously kept that back, and she was not ashamed to make it seem that she had run to the young officer on her own impulse, counting on something ... to beg him for the money. It was something tremendous! I went cold and trembled as I listened. The court was hushed, straining to catch each word. It was something without precedent. Even from a girl as willful and scornfully proud as she was, such a frank confession, such sacrifice, such giving up of herself, seemed unbelievable. And for what, and for whom? To save the man who had deceived and insulted her, and to help, however little, in saving him, by making a strong impression in his favor. And indeed, the figure of the young officer who, with a respectful bow to the innocent girl, handed her his last four thousand roubles, all he had in the world, was cast in a very sympathetic and attractive light. But ... I had a painful misgiving in my heart! I felt that slander might come of it later (and it did, in fact, it did). All over town afterwards it was repeated, with spiteful laughter, that the story was perhaps not quite complete, that is, in the statement that the officer had let the young lady leave “with nothing but a respectful bow.” People hinted that something had been left out here.

old: “Gentlemen of the jury,” began the prosecutor, “this case has caused a stir all over Russia. But why should that surprise us? What is so especially horrifying in it for us? We are so used to such crimes! That is what is truly horrible: that such dark deeds no longer horrify us. What ought to horrify us is that we have grown so used to them, and not this or that single crime. What are the causes of our indifference, of our lukewarm attitude toward such deeds, toward such signs of the times, which are ominous for an unenviable future? Is it our cynicism? Is it the premature exhaustion of mind and imagination in a society that is sinking into decay in spite of its youth? Is it that our moral principles are shattered to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I cannot answer such questions. Yet they are disturbing, and every citizen not only must, but ought to be troubled by them. Our newborn and still timid press has already done the public good service, for without it we would never have heard of the horrors of unbridled violence and moral degradation that the press keeps bringing to the notice, not only of those who attend the new jury courts set up in the present reign, but of everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Of things beside which the present case grows pale and seems almost commonplace. But what matters most is that the majority of our national crimes of violence bear witness to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it is hard to fight against it.
